description: Developing an system to evaluate potential Artemis landing zones at the lunar south pole.
summary:
At the Moon’s south pole, the Sun never rises far above the horizon. A crater rim a few kilometres away can cut a lander’s power, and a mountain can block its link to Earth. We built HELIOS LUNA, a free web tool that shows what sunlight, Earth contact and all the other important stuff a landing site will get before anyone commits to it.

Pick any site and touchdown date. HELIOS LUNA uses NASA’s LOLA terrain to work out the real horizon around the site, and NAIF SPICE to place the Sun and Earth on it hour by hour. It tells you how long you’ll have sunlight, when Earth will be in view of the Deep Space Network, and how long until the next sunset. It grades each site GO, CHECK or NO-GO, finds landing windows, and shows how close the nearest water ice is. Our results agree with JPL Horizons to within a few ten-thousandths of a degree.

The entire project is ready and is live at https://helios-luna-ls.vercel.app/
details:
HELIOS LUNA is a free web app that shows mission planners, students and the public whether a lunar landing site will have sunlight and contact with Earth, and for how long.

What it does: Pick any site and touchdown date. The app traces NASA LOLA terrain out to 300 km in 1,440 directions to build the site’s true horizon, then places the Sun and Earth on it using NAIF SPICE ephemeris. It reports sunlit hours, the longest darkness, the Earth link through the Deep Space Network or ESA Estrack, battery state, and a countdown to the next sunset and Earthset. Each site is graded GO, CHECK or NO-GO against a mission profile. The app also finds landing windows, shows how a schedule slip changes the picture, and gives the distance to the nearest permanently shadowed crater where water ice may survive. Its Map view ray-traces shadows for the whole south pole live on the GPU.

Benefits and impact: Answers that normally need ephemeris software, terrain models and expert time take seconds in a browser, with no install. Outputs are ready for engineers: a mission brief, an STK horizon mask, calendar files, GeoJSON and CSV.

Tools: TypeScript, React, Vite, Zustand, WebGL shaders and Web Workers in the browser; Python with SpiceyPy and NumPy to bake the data. Hosted on Vercel and GitHub Pages.

Creativity: GPU-rendered live shadows, exact horizons at any mast height, and water ice shown next to sunlight in the same view.

Factors we considered: Accuracy first. Twelve automated tests check the results against JPL Horizons (within 0.0002°), SPICE, PGDA maps and LROC images. We also kept the interface clear enough for non-experts. We used Claude as an AI coding assistant.
dataRefs: LRO LOLA terrain models (LDEM polar 20 m–240 m, LDEM_16 global)
NAIF SPICE toolkit and kernels (DE440, Moon PA, Earth orientation)
NASA GSFC PGDA lunar polar illumination maps (water-ice / permanent shadow)
Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LROC WAC imagery for validation)
NASA Deep Space Network station locations
NASA Artemis program (Artemis III candidate landing regions)
